name: Lions of the Great War
text: Your train passes near the Lions of the Great War, on the train's {side}, in Smethwick's High Street. Unveiled on November 4th 2018, the bronze figure of a Sikh soldier, three metres tall on a granite plinth, remembers the Sikhs of the British Indian Army who fought in the First World War.

name: Summit Bridge
text: Your train passes Summit Bridge, on the train's {side}, built in 1788 and 1789 to carry Roebuck Lane over John Smeaton's new cutting for the Birmingham Canal. The cutting lowered the canal at its summit and did away with several locks; the bridge is listed Grade II* and is also a scheduled monument.

name: Birmingham Mint
text: Your train passes near the site of the Birmingham Mint, on the train's {side}, once the world's largest privately owned mint. Starting in 1817 as a family firm making brass fittings, it went on to strike coins for France, Italy, China and much of the British Empire, and closed in 2003.

name: St Paul's Church
text: Your train passes near St Paul's Church, on the train's {side}, in Birmingham's Georgian St Paul's Square. Consecrated in 1779 and listed Grade I, it was the church of the town's early manufacturers: Matthew Boulton and James Watt had their own pews there.

name: St Philip's Cathedral
text: Your train passes near St Philip's Cathedral, on the train's {side}, on Colmore Row. Designed in the Baroque style by Thomas Archer and consecrated in 1715 as a parish church, it became the cathedral of the new Diocese of Birmingham in 1905.

name: The Old Crown
text: Your train passes near the Old Crown, on the train's {side}, a black and white timber-framed pub in Deritend that claims to be one of the oldest secular buildings in Birmingham. John Leland noted it as a “mansion house of tymber” in 1538.

name: Holy Trinity Church
text: Your train passes near the former Holy Trinity Church, on the train's {side}, at Camp Hill. Built between 1820 and 1822 by Francis Goodwin in the Gothic Revival style, it is said to have been modelled on King's College Chapel, Cambridge.

name: Curzon Street station
text: Your train passes near the entrance building of the old Curzon Street station, on the train's {side}, designed by Philip Hardwick and built in 1838 for the London and Birmingham Railway. It is among the world's oldest surviving pieces of monumental railway architecture, and is to become part of the entrance to the new HS2 station.

name: Birmingham Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Birmingham Town Hall, on the train's {side}, in Victoria Square. Opened in 1834 and listed Grade I, it was built as a home for the Birmingham Triennial Music Festival, which raised money for the General Hospital, and as a hall for public meetings.

name: Engine Arm Aqueduct
text: Your train passes near the Engine Arm Aqueduct, on the train's {side}, a single cast-iron span built by Thomas Telford in 1829. It carries a feeder, the Engine Arm, over the deep cutting of his New Main Line of the Birmingham Canal.

name: Perry Hall Park
text: Your train passes near Perry Hall Park, on the train's {side}, on the site of Perry Hall, home of the Gough family, demolished in 1927; only its moat remains. When Harry Dorsey Gough set up home in Maryland in 1774, he named his estate there Perry Hall.

name: Sandwell Valley RSPB reserve
text: Your train passes near the RSPB's Sandwell Valley nature reserve, on the train's {side}, round the edges of Forge Mill Lake, a storm water basin in a bend of the River Tame. Its bird hide stands on stilts in the lake and is reached by a drawbridge.

name: Bescot Yard
text: Your train passes Bescot Yard, on the train's {side}, the main railway freight yard of the West Midlands. Remodelled in 1966 to handle more than 4,000 wagons a day, it can be clearly seen from the junction of the M5 and M6 motorways.

name: Bescot Hall
text: Your train passes near the site of Bescot Hall, on the train's {side}, a manor house built before 1311 and first held by the Hillary family. The first house was demolished in the 18th century, and only earthworks remain, among them its moat, now a shallow hollow for most of the way round.

name: Bescot Stadium
text: Your train passes near Bescot Stadium, on the train's {side}, home of Walsall Football Club. Sir Stanley Matthews opened it on August 18th 1990; it replaced Fellows Park, a quarter of a mile away, the club's ground for 94 years.

name: Villa Park
text: Your train passes near Villa Park, on the train's {side}, home of Aston Villa since 1897. The club moved to a sports ground in a Victorian amusement park in the old grounds of Aston Hall, and the stadium has hosted 55 FA Cup semi-finals, more than any other.

name: Aston Hall
text: Your train passes near Aston Hall, on the train's {side}, a Jacobean house designed by John Thorpe and built for Sir Thomas Holte between 1618 and 1635. Bought by Birmingham Corporation in 1864, it was the first historic country house to pass into a council's hands; a hole in its staircase was made by a cannonball when Parliamentary troops attacked in 1643.

name: Spaghetti Junction
text: Your train passes Spaghetti Junction, on the train's {side}, the Gravelly Hill Interchange where the M6 meets the Aston Expressway. Opened on May 24th 1972, it has 559 concrete columns on five levels, and its nickname was coined by the Birmingham Evening Mail in 1965.

name: Washwood Heath depot
text: Your train passes near the site of the Washwood Heath depot, on the train's {side}, planned as a depot for HS2 trains. The land was once the Washwood Heath railway works, later used by Metro-Cammell and Alstom, and was cleared in 2019.

name: Battle of Saltley Gate
text: Your train passes near the scene of the Battle of Saltley Gate, on the train's {side}: in February 1972, during a national miners' strike, mass pickets closed a fuel depot here that was sending out tens of thousands of tons of coke. Its closure secured victory for the National Union of Mineworkers.

name: St Martin in the Bull Ring
text: Your train passes near St Martin in the Bull Ring, on the train's {side}, the original parish church of Birmingham, between the Bull Ring shopping centre and the markets. The present Victorian church stands on the site of one documented in 1263.

name: Birmingham Proof House
text: Your train passes the Birmingham Gun Barrel Proof House, on the train's {side}, on Banbury Street. It was set up by an Act of Parliament in 1813, at the Birmingham gun trade's request, to test that gun barrels could stand being fired before they were sold; its Jacobean-style gateway was added in 1883.

name: Fort Dunlop
text: Your train passes near Fort Dunlop, on the train's {side}, the main building of Dunlop's great tyre factory, beside the M6. The factory was built on a 120-hectare site during the First World War, and by 1954 it employed 10,000 workers.

name: Moseley Road Baths
text: Your train passes near the Public Library and Baths on Moseley Road, on the train's {side}: the library opened in 1895 and the baths in 1907. Built of red brick and terracotta, the baths are one of only three swimming pools in the country listed Grade II*.

name: St Mary's Church
text: Your train passes near St Mary's, the parish church of Moseley, on the train's {side}. Worship there goes back to a papal mandate of 1405, which allowed mass to be said in the chapel of St Mary because the parish church, at Bromsgrove, was so far away.

name: Highbury Hall
text: Your train passes near Highbury Hall, on the train's {side}, which Joseph Chamberlain had built as his Birmingham home in 1878 and lived there from 1880 until his death in 1914. He named it after Highbury in London, where he had lived as a child.

name: Stratford House
text: Your train passes near Stratford House, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house of 1601 built by Ambrose and Bridget Rotton, whose initials are carved over the porch. The London, Midland and Scottish Railway bought it in 1926 meaning to pull it down, but a public outcry saved it.

name: St Andrew's
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's, on the train's {side}, home of Birmingham City since it opened in 1906. The original ground could hold an estimated 75,000 people, and its record crowd, more than 66,000, saw a 1939 FA Cup tie against Everton.

name: Hay Hall
text: Your train passes near Hay Hall, on the train's {side}, a 15th-century hall now surrounded by a business park. A moated house was first built here by the De La Haye family in about 1275 and rebuilt in 1430; in the 16th century the timber frame was encased in brick.

name: Tyseley Locomotive Works
text: Your train passes near Tyseley Locomotive Works, on the train's {side}, on part of the Great Western Railway's old depot. It began in 1966 as a base for the Castle-class engine Clun Castle, and is now home to a large collection of steam and diesel locomotives.

name: Church of the Ascension
text: Your train passes near the Church of the Ascension, on the train's {side}, consecrated on May 25th 1704 and once known as the Job Marston Chapel after the local man who gave £1,000 to build it. It is the earliest classical church surviving in Birmingham.

name: Sarehole Mill
text: Your train passes near Sarehole Mill, on the train's {side}, a water mill on the River Cole known for its links with J. R. R. Tolkien. The present building dates from 1771, and Matthew Boulton leased the mill as early as 1755; it is one of only two working water mills in Birmingham.

name: Yardley Wood station
text: Yardley Wood station, at one end of this stretch, opened with the line on July 1st 1908 as Yardley Wood Platform, a Great Western name for a stop between a halt and a station in importance. Unlike the stations either side, it never had goods facilities.

name: Major's Green
text: Your train passes near Major's Green, on the train's {side}, the north-easternmost village in Worcestershire. Until 1962 it was part of Solihull and so in Warwickshire, and three of its four roads lead into Solihull.

name: Wythall station
text: Wythall station, at one end of this stretch, has changed its name four times: it opened as Grimes Hill Platform on July 1st 1908, and took its present name on May 6th 1974. It is just outside the West Midlands, in Worcestershire.

name: Earlswood station
text: Earlswood station, at one end of this stretch, has platforms that straddle the border between the West Midlands and Warwickshire. It opened as Earlswood Lakes in 1908 and was renamed in 1974, though The Lakes station, opened later, is nearer the village of Earlswood.

name: Earlswood Lakes
text: Your train passes near Earlswood Lakes, on the train's {side}, three reservoirs built in the 1820s to supply water to the Stratford-upon-Avon Canal, which they still do. Their northern banks mark the boundary between Warwickshire and the West Midlands.

name: The Lakes station
text: The Lakes station, at one end of this stretch, was opened by the Great Western Railway on June 3rd 1935 as a halt for fishermen and day trippers going to Earlswood Lakes. Its platforms are only a third as long as those at Earlswood.

name: St Mary Magdalene's Church, Tanworth-in-Arden
text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary Magdalene in Tanworth-in-Arden, on the train's {side}, built between the 13th century and the 1330s and listed Grade I. The singer-songwriter Nick Drake, who grew up in the village, is buried in its churchyard.

name: Beaudesert Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Beaudesert Castle, on the train's {side}, on a high mound above the village of Beaudesert. First an Iron Age fort, the hill was shaped into a Norman motte and bailey, and a stone castle there was the seat of the de Montfort family for more than a hundred years.
